{{< include _score-kit.qmd >}}

Most instruments live in one clef. A few move between two, three or even four, choosing whichever keeps
the notes on the staff. When you read a score you have to follow the switches, and for a handful of
instruments you also have to know an old convention that changes the octave.

## 1. The clef map

| Instrument | Main clef | Also | When it switches |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Viola** | alto | treble | long high passages |
| **Cello** | bass | tenor, treble | tenor for the upper register, treble for the highest |
| **Double bass** | bass | tenor, treble | solo and very high writing; *sounds an octave lower in every clef* |
| **Bassoon** | bass | tenor, (treble) | tenor for high passages; treble is rare |
| **Trombone** | bass | tenor, alto | tenor for high tenor-trombone parts; alto clef for the alto trombone and in older scores |
| **Euphonium** | bass (concert) | tenor; *or* treble in B♭ | treble clef parts are a transposition, not a clef change (see [lesson 3](score-transposition.qmd)) |
| **Horn** | treble | bass | low notes; see the octave trap below |
| **Bass clarinet** | treble | bass | depends on the edition: see below |
| **Piano, harp, celesta** | treble + bass | either clef on either staff | a hand moves into the other range |
| **Organ** | treble + bass + pedal staff | | the pedals get their own bass-clef staff |
| **Choir** | soprano, alto: treble · tenor: octave treble · bass: bass | tenor in bass clef | in closed score (two staves) the tenor shares the bass staff; see [section 5](#choir-scores-and-the-tenors-clef) |

## 2. Following a cello part

A clef change in the middle of a line is drawn small, just before the note it affects. It lasts
until the next change. This cello line climbs from bass clef through tenor into treble:

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:D clef=bass
D,, F,, A,, D, | [K:clef=tenor] F, A, D F | [K:clef=treble] A B c d | [K:clef=bass] D,4 |]
</script></div>

Notice that each switch happens where the old clef would have needed ledger lines. A good part changes
clef as rarely as it can: one long passage in tenor clef is easier than switching every bar.

## 3. The octave traps

Three conventions change the octave, and editions disagree about them. When in doubt, check the
edition's preface or compare with another part playing the same line.

**Old-style cello treble clef.** In some 18th- and 19th-century editions, when a cello part moved into
treble clef straight from bass clef, the treble-clef notes were meant **an octave lower** than written.
Modern editions write treble clef at its real pitch. If a cello treble passage looks implausibly high,
this may be why.

**Horn in bass clef, "old notation".** Horn parts in bass clef come in two kinds. In *new notation* the
horn in F sounds a fifth lower than written, in bass clef just as in treble. In *old notation* the
bass-clef notes are written an octave lower, so they sound **a fourth higher** than written. Composers
disagreed for a long time; many modern parts say "new notation" in a footnote because both are still met.

**Bass clarinet, French and German.** The bass clarinet in B♭ is now usually written in treble clef
and sounds a major ninth lower (the "French" way), so it reads exactly like a B♭ clarinet. Older German
scores (Wagner, Strauss, Mahler) often use bass clef, sounding only a major second lower, and may mix the
two in one part.

## 4. Double bass, guitar and tenor voice

These read in their normal clefs but sound an **octave lower**. That is not a clef switch, it is an
octave transposition, and it is so standard that a concert-pitch score keeps it. The guitar's and
tenor's clef is often drawn with a small 8 under the treble clef to say so. More in
[lesson 3](score-transposition.qmd).

## 5. Choir scores and the tenor's clef

A choir score has four parts, **soprano, alto, tenor and bass** (SATB), laid out in one of two ways.

**Open score: one staff per voice.** Soprano and alto read treble clef, bass reads bass clef, and the
tenor reads the **octave treble clef**: a treble clef with a small **8 underneath**. The 8 means "sounds an
octave lower than written". A tenor's written G on the second line sings the G below middle C, and the
middle C a tenor sings is written in the third space. Without the clef the tenor line would sit in the
bass staff's top ledger lines or hover across middle C; with it, the line sits in the middle of a staff.
Because the old C tenor clef has dropped out of choral music, singers often call this octave treble clef
"the tenor clef" too. Ask which one is meant.

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Open score: tenor in octave treble clef
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:G
V:S name="Soprano" clef=treble
V:A name="Alto" clef=treble
V:T name="Tenor" clef=treble-8
V:B name="Bass" clef=bass
[V:S] B A G2 | A B c B | A2 G2 |]
[V:A] G F G2 | F G E G | F2 D2 |]
[V:T] d d B2 | d d c d | d2 B2 |]
[V:B] G, D, E,2 | D, G, A, G, | D,2 G,,2 |]
</script></div>

**Closed score: two staves**, as in a hymnal. Soprano and alto share the treble staff (soprano stems up,
alto stems down); tenor and bass share the bass staff (tenor up, bass down). Here the tenor is written
**at sounding pitch in bass clef**, so the same tenor notes look an octave lower on the page than in open
score, and sit in the bass staff's upper half. Same music, same sound:

<div class="abc-ex" data-sound="piano"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Closed score: tenor in bass clef
M:4/4
L:1/4
%%score (S A) (T B)
K:G
V:S clef=treble stem=up
V:A clef=treble stem=down
V:T clef=bass stem=up
V:B clef=bass stem=down
[V:S] B A G2 | A B c B | A2 G2 |]
[V:A] G F G2 | F G E G | F2 D2 |]
[V:T] D D B,2 | D D C D | D2 B,2 |]
[V:B] G, D, E,2 | D, G, A, G, | D,2 G,,2 |]
</script></div>

**Reading tenor parts.**

- **The notes read like treble clef, an octave down.** A tenor reads the names exactly as in treble
  clef; only the sound moves. Nothing changes in the key signature.
- **Not every edition draws the 8.** Many choral editions print a plain treble clef on the tenor staff
  and expect you to know. A treble staff labelled *Tenor* (or *T.*, or *Men* in a men's part) is sung an
  octave lower, 8 or no 8. Some older editions use a **double treble clef** (two treble clefs side by
  side) for the same meaning.
- **Older scores use the C clef.** Choral music printed before the 20th century often put the tenor in
  the **tenor clef** (the C clef on the fourth line, [lesson 1](score-clefs.qmd#reading-tenor-clef)), and
  the alto and soprano in their own C clefs too. Modern editions replaced them with treble and octave
  treble.
- **Switching between scores.** A tenor who sings from a hymnal (bass clef, closed score) and from an
  octave-edition (octave treble, open score) sees the same notes in two places. Find middle C in each:
  third space in octave treble, first ledger line above the bass staff in bass clef.
- **Accompanists and conductors** reading open score at the piano play the tenor line an octave below
  what the treble clef shows; played as written, the tenors' notes would sound above the altos'.

## 6. Check yourself

Clefs shuffle at random. Aim for 20 in a row without a mistake before moving on.

<div class="sq" data-quiz="clefs"></div>
